title: Sugriva's map of the world
hookLine: four armies, four directions, and a land Hindus still walk as pilgrims
carry: tirtha: holy crossings in every direction

cards: The rains are over and the roads are open. Sugriva stands before an army gathered from every forest and mountain he rules, and he has almost nothing to hand it: a bundle of jewels, a name, and one direction.
The chariot flew south. That's all anyone knows. Somewhere beyond the forests and rivers and seas is one woman, and no one has an address.
Sugriva's answer is to split the army four ways, and to give each leader directions so detailed they fill whole chapters.

teach.b: Sugriva sends Vinata east, Sushena west, Shatabali north, and to the south, where Ravana flew, his best: Angada, with Hanuman and the old bear Jambavan.

For each direction he names rivers, mountains, kingdoms and seas, and strange places at the edge of the world. Some names are real, the Ganga, the Yamuna, the Godavari; others belong to myth. How does he know all this?

Sugriva later tells Rama: when Vali chased him, he fled everywhere, and saw the whole world while running for his life. His exile became his map. And there's a deadline: one month, or answer with your lives.
Here the story touches something Hindus still do with their feet. Many of the rivers and mountains on Sugriva's lists are tirthas, holy places.
Tirtha literally means a ford, a crossing place, and many teachers explain it this way: somewhere the line between this world and the divine is thin enough to cross.
Pilgrimage, tirtha-yatra, is one of the oldest Hindu practices.

There's even a well-known circle of four, the Char Dham, the four abodes at India's edges: Badrinath in the north, Puri in the east, Dwarka in the west, and Rameswaram in the south, which tradition links to Rama's own worship of Shiva.
Many Hindus hope to reach all four in a lifetime. Sugriva sends armies in four directions to find one person.
Pilgrims walk in four directions toward God. It meets a life now: families plan India trips around a temple, and grandparents save for a yatra.
And many read Sugriva's map this way: the roads you walked in hard years can become a map for someone else.

how: Many places named in the Ramayana are still tirthas, pilgrimage places; the Char Dham, at India's four edges (Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka, Rameswaram), is a pilgrimage many Hindus hope to complete in a lifetime.

games.q: your nani wants to see all four dhams in her lifetime. by today's story, what's the point of going so far?
o: tirtha: crossing the whole land toward God, in every direction.
games.why: Sugriva's armies crossed the world for Sita; pilgrims cross it toward God, at the four edges of India.

practice: Feel the four directions around you: in front, behind, left and right. Breathe into each in turn. Before a puja, many Hindus invite the holy rivers, the Ganga and others, into a small pot of water, so a pilgrimage comes to them.
Picture one holy place, or anywhere you once felt close to something greater, and breathe as if you stood there. Then rest in the middle of all four.

wordCard.voice: The search parties. Four armies, four directions, and a land full of tirthas, places to cross over.

orig.note: Sanskrit tīrtha: a ford or crossing place; a holy site, a place of pilgrimage.
